name: Gnaphalium Green
lede: Gnaphalium Green is a soft, pale grey-green named for Gnaphalium, the everlasting or cudweed genus whose leaves carry that same dusty tone, and recorded by Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: An everlasting's green
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* gives this hue at plate XLVII, hue 29″″, tone d, and it is also the color's first recorded date in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 placed it in block 149, a pale green [2]. Gnaphalium is the botanical genus name for the everlastings and cudweeds, small-flowered plants whose grey-green, felted leaves this color is built to describe, so the name skips an English common word for the Latin one [2].

The nearest named color is [[bluish-green|Bluish Green]], just 2.9 units away and almost indistinguishable; [[pale-oak|Pale Oak]] sits 4.2 units off, more vivid and yellower [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Gnaphalium Green appears in 543 of our 23,781 paintings, as photographed, more common than 79 percent of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 44 of 1,674 paintings, at 1.8 times the expected rate, and Niels Larsen Stevns is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 4 of his 22 works here at 5.8 times the baseline for his museums [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light rather than a shadow [3]. The earliest match is dated 1301, 611 years before Ridgway's 1912 record — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that the pigment was lifted from any plant, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].
